How the compact nursing license works for travel nurses

One license, many states. Who qualifies, what it covers and what to do when the state you want is not part of it.

For a travel nurse, the license decides the map. A multistate license opens a large part of the country at once; a single-state license means planning each move a little further ahead. Here is how to tell which you have, and how to use it.

What a compact license is

The Nurse Licensure Compact is an agreement between member states. A nurse whose primary state of residence is a member can hold one multistate license and practice in every other member state, in person or by telehealth, without applying for another license.

Who qualifies

Eligibility follows where you legally live, not where you work. If your home state is a compact member and you meet its requirements, you can apply for a multistate license there. If your home state is not a member, you hold a single-state license and apply to each new state separately.

When the state you want is not in the compact

You apply to that state's board for a license by endorsement. Expect verification of your existing license, fingerprints, a background check and a fee. Some boards issue a temporary permit while the full license is processed.

Three habits that save weeks

  • Apply as soon as you know which state you want. Boards are slowest around graduation season.
  • Keep every license number, expiry date and certification card in one folder.
  • If you move home, tell your board. Changing your primary state of residence changes which license you hold.

Membership and rules change, so always confirm the current position with the board of nursing in your home state and the state you plan to work in.
